outcome: No event since 26 January 2024 settles or moves the question for three-dimensional convex solids: the only results on the problem are local ones from 2012 to 2014 (the ball packs worse than nearby origin-symmetric solids, for lattice packings), and the in-window items I found concern the planar Reinhardt problem, covering, lattice packing minima, high-dimensional sphere packing, or a ten-result OpenAI announcement that does not touch convex solids.
problem_asks: Statement (Wikipedia, January 2024): Ulam's packing conjecture about the identity of the worst-packing convex solid. Parts: (1) For a convex solid K, the optimal packing density delta(K) is the highest density achieved by packings of congruent copies of K. The statement asks which convex solid has the lowest delta(K). (2) The conjectured answer, as the Wikipedia lead and the Kallus papers state it, is the ball: delta(K) >= delta(B3) for every convex solid K, where delta(B3) = pi/sqrt(18) ≈ 0.7405 by the Kepler theorem. (3) The identity claim is that the ball is the minimiser: that no convex solid packs less densely than the ball, and (for the identity to be exact) whether any other solid ties it. (4) The statement gives no dimension; the Wikipedia lead and infobox restrict the question to three-dimensional Euclidean space, and this record follows that restriction. The planar analogue (disk versus smoothed octagon, Reinhardt) is a different question and is not part of this bullet.

events.what_happened: Conway and Torquato, PNAS 2006 ('Packing, tiling, and covering with tetrahedra'), argued that the regular tetrahedron may not be able to pack as densely as a sphere, which would contradict Ulam's conjecture, and that it might be the convex body with the smallest possible packing density. NOT OPENED: the PMC page returned only a browser-verification screen. The statement comes from a search snippet of the abstract and from a secondary summary.
events.delivers: A candidate counterexample proposed for one solid only (the regular tetrahedron): that its optimal packing density is below the sphere's. The argument's method was not read, so this is a claim, not an established result.
events.remains: All of problem_asks. The event addresses only the tetrahedron.

checked_by.who: PNAS editorial process (refereed journal); authors Conway and Torquato
checked_by.qualification: Refereed journal of record; the authors are established researchers in packing
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the candidate. I did not open the article, so I cannot say what checks were made.

events.doubts: Superseded for this candidate. Explicit tetrahedron packings of density 4000/4671 ≈ 0.856 (Chen, Engel and Glotzer 2010; abstract opened) lie above the sphere's ≈0.7405, so the tetrahedron cannot be a counterexample in the suggested direction. This rests on those abstracts and on the 2006 snippet only.
events.direction: If correct, would cut against Ulam's conjecture for one solid (the tetrahedron). Later explicit packings cut the other way for that solid.

events.what_happened: Torquato and Jiao, 'Dense packings of the Platonic and Archimedean solids' (arXiv 0908.4107, posted 27 August 2009; Nature 460, 876-879, 2009). They use an adaptive shrinking cell optimisation to find dense packings of the Platonic solids: according to the abstract, about 0.782 for tetrahedra, 0.947 for octahedra, 0.904 for dodecahedra and 0.836 for icosahedra. They conjecture that the densest centrally symmetric Platonic and Archimedean packings are their densest lattice packings. The abstract page does not mention Ulam. A search snippet attributes a remark about Ulam's conjecture and symmetry to the full text; I did not confirm it.
events.delivers: Numerical lower bounds on the optimal packing densities of five Platonic solids, each above the sphere's ≈0.7405. This is a finite set of numerical checks. It establishes nothing about which convex solid is worst.

checked_by.who: Nature (refereed journal of record); Torquato and Jiao
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the numerical packings. Referee reports are not public.

events.doubts: The densities are outputs of a numerical optimisation, not certified bounds. The abstract does not say they are proven optimal in their families.
events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture for the five solids listed: each packs above the sphere's density.
events.object: Numerical dense packings (periodic configurations found by the adaptive shrinking cell search) of the five Platonic solids. Not reproduced in the abstract. Explicit in the sense of being a specific configuration, found by numerical search.

events.what_happened: Haji-Akbari and co-authors, Nature 2009 ('Disordered, quasicrystalline and crystalline phases of densely packed tetrahedra'). NOT OPENED: the Nature page redirected to a login screen. The values reported (a dodecagonal quasicrystal phase near 0.8324 and a crystalline approximant near 0.8503) come from a secondary summary and are unverified.
events.delivers: Per the secondary summary only: simulated dense tetrahedron packings above the sphere's density. Numerical, finite, and one solid. Does not settle the conjecture.

checked_by.who: Nature (refereed journal of record); Haji-Akbari and co-authors

events.doubts: Unverified: values and framing come from a secondary summary, and the Nature text was not readable.
events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture for tetrahedra, if the summary is right.
people: Haji-Akbari et al. (author list not verified)

events.what_happened: Chen, Engel and Glotzer, 'Dense crystalline dimer packings of regular tetrahedra' (arXiv 1001.0586, posted 5 January 2010; Discrete & Computational Geometry 44, 253, 2010). They report the densest known packing of regular tetrahedra, density 4000/4671 ≈ 0.856347: a crystal with four tetrahedra per unit cell forming two triangular dipyramids. They show it is maximal within a three-parameter family of dimer packings, and numerical compressions suggest it may be optimal for periodic cells of up to 16 tetrahedra. The abstract does not mention Ulam or the sphere density.
events.revisions: arXiv v1 5 Jan 2010; v2 6 Jan 2010; v3 25 Jul 2010; Discrete & Computational Geometry 44 (2010) 253.
events.delivers: A lower bound of 4000/4671 ≈ 0.856 on the optimal packing density of the regular tetrahedron, above the sphere's ≈0.7405. The tetrahedron is therefore not a counterexample in the suggested direction. This covers one solid and does not identify the worst one.
events.remains: All of problem_asks, including the tetrahedron's exact optimal density (the value is a lower bound) and every other solid.

checked_by.who: Discrete & Computational Geometry (refereed journal); Chen, Engel and Glotzer

events.direction: Against the tetrahedron as a counterexample, since its density is above the sphere's. Consistent with the conjecture for that solid.
events.object: The regular tetrahedron dimer crystal: a periodic packing whose unit cell holds four tetrahedra forming two triangular dipyramids, with density 4000/4671. It is explicit, a specific periodic construction, and its density can be checked by computing the cell's volume fraction. I did not compute it.

events.what_happened: de Graaf, van Roij and Dijkstra, 'Dense regular packings of irregular nonconvex particles' (arXiv 1107.0603, posted 4 July 2011; Physical Review Letters 107, 155501, 2011). The arXiv abstract concerns non-convex, irregular and punctured particles and does not mention Ulam or convex solids. A 2013 citing paper (arXiv 1307.7004, read in its full HTML rendering) says this work extended numerical verification of Ulam's conjecture to the first 8 regular prisms and antiprisms, the 92 Johnson solids and the 13 Catalan solids. I did not read the PRL text, so the verification is established only through that citing paper.
events.revisions: arXiv v1 4 Jul 2011; v2 5 Jul 2011. PRL 107, 155501 (2011) is given as the DOI record; not opened.
events.delivers: Per the citing paper only: numerical checks that no listed solid (first 8 regular prisms and antiprisms, 92 Johnson, 13 Catalan solids) packs better than the ball. These are finitely many named instances of a universal claim, and numerical rather than proofs, so under the scope test they move nothing.

checked_by.who: Physical Review Letters (refereed journal); de Graaf, van Roij and Dijkstra
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the letter. The Ulam verification is not visible in the arXiv abstract.

events.doubts: Attribution is unconfirmed. The arXiv abstract does not mention Ulam or convex solids, and the claim rests on a single citing paper's description. The 2011 paper's stated scope is non-convex particles.
events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture for the listed solids; no violation reported.

events.what_happened: Yoav Kallus, with Fedor Nazarov, posted 'In which dimensions is the ball relatively worst packing?' on arXiv on 11 December 2012 (arXiv 1212.2551 v1; announced to the Oklahoma State list on 17 December 2012). The final version, 'The 3-ball is a local pessimum for packing', is by Kallus alone (Nazarov is thanked and declined co-authorship); it appeared in Advances in Mathematics 264 (2014) 355-370. Theorem 5 of the final version, as rendered on ar5iv: there is an epsilon > 0 such that every non-ellipsoidal origin-symmetric convex solid K with (1-epsilon)B3 ⊆ K ⊆ (1+epsilon)B3 satisfies phi(K) > phi(B3), where phi is the optimal lattice packing density (the abstract speaks of packing 'using a lattice'). So the ball is a local pessimum for lattice packing among such bodies. The paper also shows that in dimensions 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 and 24 there are origin-symmetric convex bodies of arbitrarily small asphericity whose optimal lattice packing density is below that of balls.
events.revisions: v1 11 Dec 2012 (title 'In which dimensions is the ball relatively worst packing?', Kallus with Nazarov, per the 17 Dec 2012 announcement; the v1 PDF itself was not read); v2 27 Jun 2013; v3 2 Aug 2014, 'Final submitted manuscript', retitled, Kallus alone; Advances in Mathematics 264 (2014) 355-370, doi 10.1016/j.aim.2014.07.015.
events.delivers: For three-dimensional origin-symmetric convex solids within a small neighbourhood of the ball (asphericity below an epsilon the abstract does not quantify), the optimal lattice packing density exceeds the ball's: the ball is a local worst packer in that class. Restrictions: origin-symmetric only (Remark 1 of the final version says the origin-non-symmetric case remains open); lattice packings only; local, i.e. small asphericity; three dimensions for this statement. The higher-dimensional part (4-8 and 24) shows the ball is not a local worst packer there, which is outside this bullet's dimension.
events.remains: The global statement: that the ball minimises the optimal packing density delta among all convex solids in R3. Left open: origin-non-symmetric solids; general (non-lattice) packing density; solids of large asphericity. Only the local lattice statement for origin-symmetric solids is established.

checked_by.who: Advances in Mathematics (Elsevier), a refereed journal of record; referees not named in the sources
checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted and published the paper in 2014. Referee reports are not public.

checked_by.what_they_did: Digested the local result and reported the conjecture as still open. The post does not work through the proof. Per the post, Kallus later commented that the three-dimensional case is 'mysterious'.

events.time_since_posted: 13 years 10 months since v1; 12 years since journal publication
events.direction: Consistent with Ulam's conjecture locally: no origin-symmetric body close to the ball packs worse under lattice packing. It does not settle the global conjecture. Its higher-dimensional part cuts against the analogous claim in dimensions 4-8 and 24.
events.object: No single object for the three-dimensional result. It is an inequality for origin-symmetric solids in a neighbourhood of the ball, proved by perturbation arguments (the perfection and eutaxy machinery of the paper, per its own description). For dimensions 4-8 and 24, the paper exhibits families of origin-symmetric convex bodies of arbitrarily small asphericity whose optimal lattice packing density is below the ball's. From the parts of the text I read, I did not establish whether these are explicit or non-constructive.
people: Yoav Kallus (Princeton, Center for Theoretical Science, per the ar5iv rendering)

events.what_happened: Yoav Kallus, 'When is the ball a local pessimum for covering?' (arXiv 1301.5895, posted January 2013; the day is not recorded in what I read). It concerns covering, not packing: among point-symmetric shapes, the ball is a local pessimum for lattice covering in three dimensions, but not in four or five. The text I read does not mention Ulam or the packing conjecture.
events.revisions: Journal publication given in search results as Discrete & Computational Geometry (2015); not opened.
events.delivers: A covering result in dimensions 3, 4 and 5. It is a different question (covering density, not packing density) and says nothing about the worst packing convex solid. Discarded for this bullet.

events.what_happened: Yoav Kallus, 'Pessimal packing shapes' (arXiv 1305.0289, posted 1 May 2013; revised 9 December 2014; Geometry & Topology 19 (2015) 343-363). It asks which convex shapes fill least space under densest packing, focuses on local minima because global minima appear out of reach, and proves two new results. In two dimensions, the regular heptagon is a local minimum of the double-lattice packing density. In three dimensions, the directional derivative of the double-lattice density at the ball is positive in every direction (Theorem 3 as rendered: for a non-ball three-dimensional body K in minimal-mean-width position, the double-lattice density of (1-lambda)B + lambda K exceeds the ball's by more than beta(K) lambda for small lambda). The rendering also reports that the paper says showing the ball is a local minimum of the full density delta remains open, and it attributes the conjecture that the ball minimises delta among three-dimensional convex bodies to Ulam.
events.revisions: v1 1 May 2013 (Kallus alone); v2 9 Dec 2014; Geometry & Topology 19 (2015) 343-363, doi 10.2140/gt.2015.19.343.
events.delivers: Local statements for the double-lattice packing density, not the full density delta: in two dimensions the regular heptagon is a local minimum, and in three dimensions the ball is a local minimum of the double-lattice density. Both are local (small perturbations) and concern a restricted class of packings. Neither establishes the ball as the minimiser of delta in R3.
events.remains: The global statement that the ball minimises the full packing density delta among three-dimensional convex solids; the local statement for delta itself (the paper says open, per the rendering read); non-double-lattice packings. The two-dimensional heptagon result addresses a different question.

checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper in 2015. Referee reports are not public.

events.what_happened: Thomas Hales and Koundinya Vajjha, 'Packings of Smoothed Polygons' (arXiv 2405.04331, posted 7 May 2024; a 283-page book, math.OC with math.MG cross-list). Using optimal control theory they prove Mahler's first conjecture: the most unpackable centrally symmetric convex disk in the plane is a smoothed polygon. The abstract states that Mahler's second conjecture, identical to the Reinhardt conjecture (the smoothed octagon), remains open. It notes that some proofs are computer-assisted using a computer algebra system.
events.delivers: A planar result: the most unpackable centrally symmetric convex disk is a smoothed polygon. This is two-dimensional and concerns the Reinhardt-type question, not the worst-packing convex solid in R3. Discarded for this bullet.
events.remains: The planar Reinhardt conjecture stays open per the abstract. All of the three-dimensional question is untouched.
events.direction: None on the three-dimensional question. It is about the planar analogue.

events.what_happened: Boaz Klartag, 'Lattice packing of spheres in high dimensions using a stochastically evolving ellipsoid' (arXiv 2504.05042, v1 7 April 2025, v2 25 January 2026). In every dimension n there is an origin-symmetric ellipsoid of volume c·n² containing no nonzero point of Z^n, giving a lattice sphere packing of density at least c·n²·2^(-n); earlier constructions reached at most about C·n·log n·2^(-n). The abstract page does not discuss convex bodies generally or Ulam's conjecture.
events.revisions: v1 7 Apr 2025; v2 25 Jan 2026 (current). A search snippet says the paper was accepted by Inventiones in February 2026; not verified.
events.delivers: A lower bound on lattice sphere packing density in high dimensions. It concerns balls in high dimension, not the worst convex solid in R3. Discarded for this bullet.
events.object: An origin-symmetric ellipsoid of volume c·n² with no nonzero lattice points, constructed by a stochastically evolving ellipsoid argument. The abstract does not say whether the construction is explicit; I did not establish it.

events.what_happened: Bukh, Gao, Liu, Pikhurko and Sun, 'Covering large-dimensional Euclidean spaces by random translates of a given convex body' (arXiv 2510.25685, math.CO with math.MG cross-list; v1 29 October 2025, v2 17 August 2026). It concerns covering R^n by translates, in large dimension: ball coverings with density about (1/2)n ln n, a multiplicity bound of about 1.7956 n ln n, and a limit below (1/2)n ln n for the random construction for any convex body. Packing density appears only as a comparison (a cube is the worst body for the random construction).
events.delivers: Covering results in large dimension. This is a different question from the packing density of three-dimensional convex solids, and it does not identify the worst-packing solid. Discarded for this bullet.
events.direction: None on the three-dimensional packing question.

events.what_happened: Mei Han, Martin Henk and Fei Xue, 'Packing minima of convex bodies' (arXiv 2601.13937, math.MG, posted 20 January 2026; one version). It extends the lattice-based packing minima of Henk, Schymura and Xue (2021), the counterparts of the covering minima of Kannan and Lovasz, to all convex bodies containing the origin in their interior. It proves new volume inequalities and computes packing minima for some special bodies. The abstract page does not mention balls, three-dimensional bodies, or AI.
events.delivers: Results on lattice-based packing minima, a different quantity from the optimal packing density of a solid. Discarded for this bullet.
events.direction: None on the three-dimensional packing question.

events.what_happened: OpenAI announced ten results in mathematics and theoretical computer science, with Lean certificates in the openai/ten-proofs repository; press coverage credits an internal model called Astra (names used in coverage include 'Astra', 'OpenAI's Astra model' and 'GPT-6 Astra'). Item 1 (SpherePacking.lean) improves asymptotic upper bounds on high-dimensional sphere packing density, reaching the Cohn-Elkies threshold. Item 8 (EhrhartVolumeInequality.lean) concerns the maximal volume of a convex body whose centroid is its only interior lattice point. No item concerns the worst-packing convex solid in R3. I read the repository README, not the manuscript, which I could not read. Press reports give about $2,000 for the ten results.

events.delivers: Nothing on this problem. The sphere-packing item concerns balls in high dimension; the Ehrhart item concerns lattice-point volume. Discarded for this bullet.
events.direction: None on the three-dimensional packing question.

disputes.summary: Martin Gardner's 1995 postscript reports that Ulam told him in 1972 that he suspected the sphere was the worst case of dense packing of identical convex solids; the original wording says only that Ulam 'suspected' it. Kallus (arXiv 1212.2551) names the claim Ulam's packing conjecture. The Wikipedia article treats the step from remark to conjecture as a later interpretation.

summary: I ran 40 web searches and opened about 25 pages, including full HTML renderings of the key Kallus papers (the PDFs were binary through WebFetch). No event since 26 January 2024 settles or moves the three-dimensional question. No proof, counterexample or AI-generated claim about this problem turned up on arXiv, Wikipedia, the n-Category Cafe, the OpenAI ten-proofs repository or the talk and benchmark pages I could reach. The events in the record are older. Kallus (arXiv 1212.2551, final in Advances in Mathematics 2014) proves that for origin-symmetric convex solids with small asphericity the optimal lattice packing density exceeds the ball's, so the ball is a local worst packer in that class; the same paper says the ball is not a local worst packer in dimensions 4-8 and 24. Kallus's 2013 'Pessimal packing shapes' (Geometry & Topology 2015) gives the same kind of local statement for double-lattice density in R3, and per the rendering I read, says the local statement for the full density is open. Both are local, lattice-only, and origin-symmetric; the 2012 paper's Remark 1 says the origin-non-symmetric case is open. The Wikipedia article, read through a summariser rather than verbatim, still lists the full conjecture as open. Human checking: the local results are refereed journal papers with no public reports; the only expert digest I found is John Baez's 2014 blog post, which reports the conjecture as open and summarises the local result without working through the proof. I found no later paper that cites them as settling anything, and no 2024-2026 paper that treats the three-dimensional problem as resolved. The numerical work (Torquato and Jiao 2009; Chen, Engel and Glotzer 2010; de Graaf et al. 2011) checks finitely many solids and moves nothing under the scope test. The tetrahedron results do rule the tetrahedron out as a counterexample, since its density is at least 0.856 against the sphere's 0.7405, but that is one case. The in-window items are: Hales and Vajjha (May 2024, planar Reinhardt, with computer algebra); Klartag (April 2025, high-dimensional lattice sphere packing); Bukh et al. (October 2025, covering); Han, Henk and Xue (January 2026, lattice packing minima); and OpenAI's ten Astra proofs (August 2026, whose sphere-packing item is high-dimensional). I recorded each as a discarded event with its reason. On AI: no source credits an AI system with anything on this problem. The 'numerical computation' in Kallus's Remark 3 is a Fourier-coefficient calculation with no system named. Close calls: (a) whether Kallus's local theorem moves a quantity the problem names. It concerns lattice density of nearby solids, not the full optimal packing density delta, and it establishes a local inequality, not the minimum. I have recorded that scope and left the weight to the judging pass. (b) Dating: I used the 2012 arXiv v1 date, not the 2014 journal date, per the DEEP_DIVE rule. (c) Attribution: the 1972 remark is a private conversation reported in 1995, so the conjecture's origin is a later interpretation. Searches for AI-generated claims (AlphaEvolve, FunSearch, Gemini Deep Think, GPT-5, Epoch AI benchmarks, the DeepMind formal-conjectures repository) returned no item on this problem.
competing_reading: Read Kallus's 2012 theorem as moving the quantity the problem asks for. The conjecture's own inequality is delta(K) >= delta(B3), and the theorem proves the strict inequality phi(K) > phi(B3) for every nearby origin-symmetric K. So within that neighbourhood the ball is strictly worse than its neighbours, and on this reading the result is partial progress on a named quantity rather than a result about a neighbouring question. Against it: phi is the lattice density, not the general packing density delta; the neighbourhood is epsilon-small and origin-symmetric; and the paper's own Remark 1 says the non-symmetric case is open. I have not weighed this.
what_would_settle_it: (1) A full-text reading of arXiv 1212.2551 and 1305.0289 (the PDFs were unreadable through WebFetch; I used ar5iv renderings), to confirm how phi and delta are defined, the value of epsilon, and whether any local statement covers general (non-lattice) packing density. (2) The de Graaf, van Roij and Dijkstra PRL text, to see whether the prism, Johnson and Catalan verifications appear there. (3) A full-text search of arXiv math.MG for 'Ulam', 'pessimal', 'worst packing' and 'local pessimum' from January 2024 to date, and the Wikipedia article's revision history since January 2024. (4) The DeepMind formal-conjectures repository and the Epoch AI open-problem list, searched directly for this problem (GitHub code search needed a login; Epoch's list was not reachable). (5) The OpenAI ten-proofs manuscript read as text, to confirm no convex-solid item.

events.credibility_reason: The suggestion that the tetrahedron packs worse than the ball was overtaken by explicit tetrahedron packings of density about 0.856; the paper itself was not opened.
The Ulam verification is attributed to this paper only by one citing paper; the paper's own abstract concerns non-convex particles.

judgement.why: The statement asks which convex solid minimises the optimal packing density, which is a universal claim (the ball) over all 3D convex solids. Numerical dense packings of specific solids (Platonic, tetrahedron dimer, Johnson/Catalan checks) each show one or finitely many solids beating the ball, so they are instances. The Conway–Torquato suggestion settles nothing. The close call is Kallus 2012 (and 2013): the competing reading treats it as partial progress. I scored it variant because it proves a local inequality for lattice density phi, not for the general packing density delta the conjecture concerns, and only for origin-symmetric bodies. Proving something about a different quantity changes the question rather than restricting it. A local theorem about delta itself would have been a case. All post-snapshot items concern the planar Reinhardt analogue, high-dimensional sphere packing, covering, or packing minima, so they are variants; the OpenAI announcement does not touch the problem, so it is none. No AI system contributed mathematics to any event.
judgement.doubts: Kallus 2012 could be read as a case (a local restriction) rather than a variant. It is scored variant because phi is lattice density rather than delta; if lattice density were taken to be the question's quantity, it would be a pre-snapshot case, which still leaves the problem open. The journal publications are taken as digestion of the published arguments. They are not verification of the numerical optima.
